papers.title: Predicting resistance to synthetic lethal therapies in cancer
authors: Yazar, M., Lord, C. J., Ryan, C. J.
papers.abstract: Background Synthetic lethality (SL) occurs when an alteration in one gene renders cells vulnerable to inhibition of another, offering a strategy for targeted cancer therapy. PARP inhibitors represent the first clinically approved synthetic lethal therapy, and numerous additional candidates are now in clinical trials. Unfortunately, resistance to these therapies is common and impairs their overall effectiveness. Although there is a growing understanding of the factors that predict synthetic lethal interactions, the prediction of mechanisms driving resistance to these effects remains largely unstudied. Here, we sought to determine whether SL resistance could be predicted a priori using protein-protein interaction networks integrated with additional molecular profiles. Methods We curated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 chemogenetic resistance screens spanning ten unique SL biomarker-target pairs. For each pair, we extracted resistance genes and computed features capturing protein-protein interactions, gene expression, and essentiality. We compared these features between resistance and non-resistance genes and developed a random forest classifier to predict resistance. Model performance was assessed using random-split and structured leave-one-out schemes based on biomarkers, targets, and SL pairs to ensure robust generalisation. Independent validation of the model was performed by assessing its ability to predict resistance to two SL therapies currently in clinical trials, MTAP-PRMT5 and ATM-ATR. Results Resistance genes were significantly enriched among the protein-protein interaction partners of SL pairs across multiple datasets, suggesting functional interaction networks can aid the prioritisation of resistance mechanisms. Resistance genes tended to be more co-expressed with their associated target and also displayed distinct essentiality patterns. Although no individual feature was strongly predictive, integrating all features in a random forest model improved discrimination between resistance and non-resistance genes. Under leave-one-SL-pair-out cross-validation - our most stringent test of generalisation - the model achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.72 across ten pairs (range 0.57-0.91; mean average precision ~9%); a random train-test split gave a higher AUROC (~0.78) that we treat as an optimistic upper bound, since biomarkers and targets are shared across folds. Average precision remained low in absolute terms, reflecting the inherent challenge of predicting extremely rare resistance events (<1% of genes). Conclusions Resistance to synthetic lethal therapies arises, at least in part, from predictable patterns of network connectivity, transcriptional coordination, and context-dependent essentiality. Our integrative framework provides a computational approach for anticipating resistance mechanisms across the expanding landscape of synthetic lethal therapies, offering a foundation for designing more durable and effective combination treatments.

papers.title: BioMod: Biological Module Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Modeling
authors: Meng, L., Zhu, J., Han, B., Zang, Y., Li, W., Zong, K., Zhong, J., Yang, Y., Liu, J., Jia, J., Sun, R., Yu, G., Han, J., Chen, Y., Zhang, L., Xu, J.
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.

papers.title: Deep-learning-driven tumor microenvironment profiling improves immunotherapy response prediction
authors: Wang, R. H., Benard, B. A., Ilerten, I., Zdravkovic, S., Al-Humadi, R., Nasr, S., Howitt, B., Gentles, A. J.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the management of many cancers, such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), yet durable clinical benefit is achieved in only a subset of patients. Immunotherapy outcomes are governed by the multicellular tumor microenvironment (TME), through the structured and directional interplay of regulatory programs and ligand-receptor communications. Yet most existing methods for immunotherapy response prediction rely on independent signatures or cell types and fail to model the structured and directional signaling network within the TME. To address this gap, we introduce EcoNet, a computational framework that first models ecosystems consisting of co-occurring cell states, then constructs intercellular and intracellular signaling networks based on the ecosystems, and applies a graph attention network to derive embeddings from the signaling network for immunotherapy response prediction. Pretrained on 2,532 pan-cancer immunotherapy samples across multiple cohorts, EcoNet outperformed existing prediction methods by 7.5-19.9% and marker-based signatures by 4.4-21.2% in AUC, and its high-attention genes were enriched among those required for T-cell-mediated tumor killing in an independent CRISPR screen; applied to ccRCC with disease-specific fine-tuning, it stratified an independent ccRCC cohort by clinical outcome (P=0.024). Biologically, high-attention genes capture an interferon-responsive program that enhances antigen presentation and immune infiltration. To validate these findings, we curated a ccRCC clinical cohort profiled with CosMx single-cell spatial transcriptomics (46 samples, ~450,000 cells) and found the response-associated TME configuration identified by EcoNet localized to immune-enriched niches, supporting the response stratification. These results establish EcoNet as a generalizable framework for TME-informed therapeutic response prediction, readily extensible to other cancer types and therapeutic contexts.

authors: Srivastava, S. P., Saxena, V., Singh, D., Singh, H., Singh, R. K.
papers.abstract: Batch active learning for ligand discovery requires a recurring decision about whether to exploit high predicted affinity, reduce model uncertainty, or broaden chemical coverage. papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) that segment from language must pass the location of the referent to a pixel decoder. New Predictor Urinary TPA-derived FABP3/APOA1 ratio (AKI^TPA index). papers.title: Optimizing copy number profiles for tumor cell phylogeny inference from low-coverage single-cell sequencing data
authors: Ahmed, N., Weiner, S., Payne, C., Bansal, M. S.
papers.abstract: Motivation: Accurate reconstruction of tumor cell phylogenies is crucial for understanding cancer evolutionary dynamics, inferring intra-tumor heterogeneity, and designing effective and personalized cancer treatment strategies. One of the most promising and cost-effective approaches for reconstructing tumor phylogenies for large numbers of cells is to use copy number alteration (CNA) data obtained from low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing of sampled tumor cells. However, error and uncertainty in inferred copy number profiles (CNPs), resulting from low sequence coverage, can have a drastic negative effect on the reconstruction accuracy of tumor cell phylogenies. Results: In this work, we show that careful selection of bin size, a critical tuning parameter for inferring CNPs, is necessary to maximize the accuracy of tumor cell phylogeny inference. Specifically, we (i) use three previously published low-coverage single-cell DNA sequencing datasets from real tumors to demonstrate that even small changes in bin size can have a drastic impact on downstream tumor phylogeny reconstruction, (ii) show that this effect persists even when using simulated low-coverage datasets generated under idealized conditions with minimal noise, and (iii) propose a simple computational approach to select bin sizes that maximize tumor phylogeny accuracy. Our experiments span a wide range of bin sizes and account for the impact of various factors including coverage-level, phylogeny reconstruction method, and CNP inference method, and explicitly account for phylogenetic reconstruction uncertainty. Our evaluation of the proposed computational approach for bin size selection shows that it can significantly improve tumor cell phylogeny reconstruction accuracy compared to baseline methods. authors: Schreurs, L. D., Barz, J., Nguyen, T.-H., Schmedding, J., Lobastova, L., Hoelker, P., Seeger-Nukpezah, T., Lackmann, J.-W., Hollenbeck, J. C., Ising, C., Kahlert, U., Timmer, M., Goldbrunner, R., Neuschmelting, V., Nguyen, P.-H.
papers.abstract: Tumour-associated microglia are major regulators of the immune microenvironment in brain malignancies, yet the early mechanisms by which tumour-derived signals shape their immune phenotype remain poorly understood. We used quantitative proteomic analysis on microglia upon tumour exposure and observed extensive remodelling of the microglial proteome following exposure to tumour-conditioned media, indicating that soluble mediators represent the dominant drivers of early microglial activation. Microglia reprogramming was characterized by coordinated upregulation of inflammatory mediators together with proteins involved in antigen presentation and T-cell regulation, including MHC-I, PD-L1 and Galectin-9. Flow cytometric validation using multiple murine and human cell models confirmed the increased expression of PD-L1 and MHC-I on microglia following exposure to tumour-derived conditioned media. Subsequently, tumour-conditioned microglia promoted expression of the inhibitory receptors PD-1 and TIM-3 on T-cells after coculture. Importantly, integration of publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets and cell-cell communication analysis further demonstrated that this immune-regulatory program is recapitulated in microglia from patients with brain tumours. Together, our findings identify an early, soluble factor-driven microglial activation program that precedes direct tumour contact and integrates inflammatory activation with immune checkpoint regulation. These results provide a mechanistic framework for the early establishment of an immunosuppressive brain tumour microenvironment and highlight microglial immune checkpoint pathways as potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
papers.abstract: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.

papers.title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
papers.abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

papers.title: PhySeqNet: physics-informed fluorescent foci detection for BARseq spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: BARseq enables spatially resolved gene-expression profiling across intact tissue, but its sensitivity depends on accurate detection and decoding of dense fluorescent rolonies. Existing spot-calling approaches can be conservative where signals overlap, while supervised deep learning is limited by the lack of reliable manual ground truth in real tissue images. Here we present PhySeqNet, a physics-informed deep learning framework for annotation-free fluorescent foci detection in BARseq. PhySeqNet trains U-Net detectors entirely on semi-synthetic images generated from an instrument-matched optical model combined with real sample-free experimental noise, and is integrated into pyBARseq, a modular Python pipeline for BARseq analysis. PhySeqNet achieved high detection performance on held-out simulated data across wavelength bands. On real tissue images, where ground truth is unavailable, we evaluated detections by forward-model reconstruction: PhySeqNet with conservative barcode-aware non-maxima suppression (NMSB) achieved higher reconstruction fidelity (NCC and MS-SSIM) than the BarDensr single-shot estimator, tuned classical spot detectors, and a pretrained deep-learning detector. In the analyzed brain section, PhySeqNet with NMSB yielded a median of 51 counts per cell versus 47 for BarDensr, with a similar number of genes detected per cell. The recovered transcripts produced spatial expression patterns qualitatively consistent with Allen MERFISH reference data and preserved cell-type composition after scANVI label transfer. These results show that physics-informed simulation can train practical, annotation-free detectors that improve BARseq sensitivity without disrupting downstream biological interpretation.
